newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-SCHALKE TAKE 1-0 LEAD IN UEFA CUP FINAL.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SCHALKE TAKE 1-0 LEAD IN UEFA CUP FINAL.

text.p: A spectacular goal from Belgian Marc Wilmots kept alive Schalke's dream of making European soccer history when they beat Inter Milan 1-0 at home in the first leg of the UEFA Cup final on Wednesday.

Just as a dismal game seemed to be heading towards a goalless draw, Wilmots picked up the ball in the middle of the Inter half in the 70th minute, took a few strides towards the edge of the box and fired the ball low into the left-hand corner.

Apart from that piece of brilliance, Schalke, who have never been in a European final and last picked up a domestic trophy back in 1972, did not produce any goalscoring chances in a match which rarely got above the standard of a mediocre domestic league encounter.
But the goal gives the Germans some hope to take to Milan for the second leg in two weeks when Inter will be looking to win the trophy for the third time after 1991 and 1994.
"We can be happy that we have scored a goal and we have won," Schalke coach Huub Stevens said. "We'll go to Milan and try to score. But if we can hold them we will win it."

Inter, who were missing French defender Jocelyn Angloma, English midfielder Paul Ince and Frenchman Youri Djorkaeff because of suspension, also struggled to get their game together and managed just one dangerous shot on goal.
The Italians are sure to take the game to Schalke in the second leg in the San Siro and will be reasonably satisfied with Wednesday's result.

Their English coach Roy Hodgson was optimistic about the return leg. "It wouldn't be the first time that a team has lost away from home and then turned the result around. I would have been quite relaxed about a 0-0," he said.

Nevertheless, the Schalke fans, who have been through some depressing times in the last two decades with several relegations from the Bundesliga, celebrated the win with passion. Despite pouring rain and cool temperatures, most of the capacity crowd refused to leave the stadium at the end.
Schalke, a major force in German football during the Second World War, have not won a trophy of any note since they picked up the German Cup in 1972.
This was by far the biggest night of their history. A crowd of 56,824 was packed into Gelsenkirchen's Park stadium in the heart of Germany's industrial Ruhr.
But the crowd had little to shout about for most of the match when the football was far from European class.
Both sides played very defensively and tactically. Apart from long-range shots from Ingo Anderbruegge and Olaf Thon, the home side hardly threatened the Italian goal at all in the first half.

Inter's best chance of the match came just before the interval when forward Maurizio Ganz broke free on the left-hand side of the box and forced Schalke keeper Jens Lehmann to tip his shot over the bar.

Apart from the goal the only other significant moment of the match came in the 15th minute when Inter sweeper Fabio Galante received his second yellow card of the competition for handling the ball. He will miss the second leg.
